script:
Counsellor: Good morning, Sara. What concerns you most about starting university next year?
Sara: I am excited about engineering, but I cannot compare different courses confidently.
Counsellor: Have you checked university websites, or mainly friends' opinions online?
Sara: Online comments about entry requirements seem inconsistent and sometimes contradict what my teachers have told me.
Counsellor: Requirements change. Check official course pages and record when you read them.
Sara: Should I compare degree names or examine what students actually study?
Counsellor: Read module descriptions and look for projects, laboratories and supervised training.
Sara: Do first-year students receive help with unfamiliar academic expectations?
Counsellor: Universities may offer orientation sessions, workshops and advisers. Confirm each service directly.
Sara: My cousin says university students must solve every problem alone. Is that true?
Counsellor: No. Independence includes recognising when you need reliable information and appropriate help.
Sara: I worry about organising time without my familiar school timetable.
Counsellor: Plan a week including classes, independent study, exercise, family and sleep.
Sara: What if group members disagree about completing an assignment?
Counsellor: Agree on responsibilities, listen respectfully and consult a tutor when necessary.
Sara: Would visiting a campus help me decide where to apply?
Counsellor: Yes. An open day introduces facilities and opportunities to meet current students.
Sara: I want to prepare questions rather than just take photographs.
Counsellor: Ask how students revise, use library resources and contact academic staff.
Sara: Accommodation and transport may affect my family's budget as much as tuition.
Counsellor: Compare realistic costs and check whether financial support is available.
Sara: Other students seem certain about their futures, while I still have questions.
Counsellor: Uncertainty is normal. Careful research is better than pretending to know everything.
Sara: I will prepare a table of entry requirements, course content, support and expenses.
Counsellor: Good. Keep your sources and update the table when information changes.
Sara: Thank you. A clear process feels better than relying on rumours.
Counsellor: Bring your questions after the campus visit, and we can review the evidence together with your family's practical concerns.
Sara: I will ask my family which practical arrangements need investigation before deciding.

questions.stem: Which subject does Sara hope to study?
Where should Sara check entry requirements?
What does the counsellor say independence includes?
What could help Sara experience a university campus?
What does Sara plan to prepare?
